Read the modules the table points to (in-depth, by-domain, reporting, word-list, question-bank). The source theory file named in `word-list.md` is not supplied, so where the skill leans on it I work from the skill's own wording. Report below.

---

## 1. The question, frozen

The paper answers several. Central, by its opening sentence: *given that posthuman civilizations would have enormous computing power, at least one of (1) f_P ≈ 0, (2) f_I ≈ 0, (3) f_sim ≈ 1 is true* — and so the untroubled belief "we will likely become posthuman ancestor-simulators" is false unless we are now simulated. Range: any civilization reaching our level. Kind of question: an argument's — do the starting points force the conclusion, and do they force the opposite just as well? The title's question, "are *you* in a simulation?", is answered by a **separate** step (the indifference principle, §V). I record that as a second claim and keep it from drifting into the first.

## 2. The parts

**Jobs** (mostly *given* in the abstract and §I): the conclusion must hold as a disjunction, not one answer; it must survive a huge spread of time-scales and cost estimates; substrate-independence is imported. My *added* jobs are the flip and "name a gauge for (1)/(2)".

**Parts, in the owner's words:** substrate-independence; the computing estimates; the counting identity (\*); f_I and N_I; the trichotomy (1)/(2)/(3); the "bland indifference principle"; the "roughly even credence" remark; the DOOM and convergence interpretations.

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | By what |
|---|---|---|
| Substrate-independence | **Borrowed** | Rests on a position in philosophy of mind, cited not tested ("we shall here take it as a given"). |
| N_I extremely large | **Held** | Remove it and (\*) can give f_sim ≈ 1/2 with f_P, f_I both substantial — none of (1)–(3) holds. Held with a wide margin, as claimed. Source estimates are fitted (retina, synapses) but used far inside their error. |
| Counting identity (\*) | **Held** | Arithmetic, from the definition of f_sim. |
| Trichotomy (1)/(2)/(3) | **Held** | Follows from (\*) plus N_I large. Real work: it rules out "f_P substantial, f_I substantial, f_sim small". |
| (1) f_P ≈ 0 | **Loose** | Any extinction story does. No gauge named. |
| (2) f_I ≈ 0 | **Loose** | Interchangeable convergence stories (ban, lost desire, enforced law); each swaps for the others and (2) still holds. No gauge. |
| (1) and (2) together | **Two routes** | Two ungauged branches absorb any evidence against (3). |
| (3) f_sim ≈ 1 | **Held if** | Held by (\*) given N_I large, and by the indifference principle — itself in doubt. The paper concedes (3) has few pokes of its own. |
| Bland indifference principle | **Borrowed** | Rests on *Anthropic Bias*, cited not tested. This is where "most minds are simulated" becomes "you likely are". |
| "Roughly even credence between (1),(2),(3)" | **Loose**, provenance **asserted** | No argument; swap "even" for any split and nothing breaks. |
| DOOM from (1) | **Held if** | Follows only if (1) is true. |

## 4. Whole-explanation checks

**Flip.** Had we found ourselves not in a simulation, the answer would be (1) or (2); had we found ourselves in one, (3). Both outcomes are covered — at the level of the disjunction. It escapes vacuity only through the one thing it forbids: f_P and f_I both substantial with f_sim small. A real cut, but a slice out of the middle, not a prediction.

**Direction.** The counting runs forward and correctly. The credence step runs from a frequency to a personal credence — a backward move ("what can I tell from where I find myself"). The paper says so; fine, if the question is kept as that backward one.

**Answer hidden in the starting points.** Not in the arithmetic. But "you are probably simulated" is close to N_I large plus the indifference principle; the principle is the load-bearing premise, and it is borrowed. The paper places and argues for it (junk DNA, betting) rather than hiding it.

**Pairs that pull.** (1) and (3) pull, by the paper's own closing remark: if simulating a posthuman civilization is prohibitively costly, a simulation would be terminated before reaching posthumanity — hoping for (3) raises the chance of termination, pushing towards (1). Also the indifference principle pulls against the Doomsday argument; the paper draws the line at "no information about which group". What would show the line misplaced is a case where the bland principle makes an independently checkable prediction — none is offered.

**Catch-alls and gauges.** (1) and (2) are catch-alls with no gauge. This is the main soft spot: the disjunction absorbs any failure of (3) with nothing measurable.

**Change list.** Openly covered: time-scale, cost estimates across orders of magnitude, any f_P, f_I. Left out: how to tell the disjuncts apart; what would falsify the indifference principle. §VI partly states this limit ("richer empirical implications" later), so it is stated, not silent — but thin.

**Rivals.** The nearest rival denies the indifference step: "frequency tells you nothing about your own credence; you are a specific observer with actual information." No change on the list separates it from the paper's step; the two differ exactly by the borrowed principle. At this level they are one claim; a finer question is a new one.

**Provenance.** *Fitted:* the brain-cost estimates. *Built:* the counting and the disjunction structure. *Asserted:* the even-credence remark, and by adoption substrate-independence.

## 5. What would make it hardest to vary

Give (1) or (2) a gauge. The paper knows the move — the simulated hypothesis "will come to have a much richer set of empirical implications" once posthuman motivations are known. Until then (2) accepts any story, so two unmeasured escape hatches protect the disjunction. Naming one measurement that would show which branch holds would tighten it more than any other cut. Second: state how the error grows with the size of the estimate, not just that it is tolerable.

## 6. What this does not show

Held is not true. A very hard-to-vary arithmetic core says nothing about whether substrate-independence or the indifference principle are right. Loose is not false: (1) may be true.

## 7. One next step

Write down one measurement that would separate (1) from (2), and the reading that would move the paper's own credence. If none can be named, mark both as ungauged catch-alls.
